entries.content:
These are the ninth through eleventh entries in a symposium of responses to the 2026 midterm elections.

Christopher Hooks • Francisco Cantú • Aslı Ü. Bâli and Aziz Rana

Lone Star Pastoral

Christopher Hooks

In January the state of Texas will experience a changeover in political power practically on the scale of a color revolution. Before the November election the question had been whether the Democrat James Talarico might win the Senate seat vacated by Lyndon Baines Johnson and lost to his party in a famous 1961 special election. This would have been painful enough, to Republicans. I was listening to an audio hangout on the site formally known as Twitter two weeks before the election when a conservative activist, not even one from Texas, was asked what it would feel like to watch Texas flip blue in this one narrow sense. “Bro, it would be like watching a man make beautiful love to my wife.”

The night of November 3, then, must have been exquisitely painful; I hope he survived. All seven statewide political offices on the ballot went to Democrats, from the Senate and the governor’s office—until now held by the imperial and cruel Greg Abbott—to lesser roles whose Democratic nominees were underfunded, little-known, and hardly able to contest their races. Every statewide judicial race was won by Democrats. After January the moribund Texas Supreme Court will consist of seven women and two men, and the chief justice, Maggie Ellis, is bisexual. Ben Flores, the land commissioner who will be overseeing the Alamo, among many other responsibilities, is a graduate of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México. Sarah Eckhardt, the comptroller who will oversee the eighth-largest economy in the world, is a Buddhist who served for years as an actress in David Mamet’s theatrical company.

This was all as hard for me to accept as it probably was for the guy on X. The Republican Party of Texas, which I have spent fifteen years covering as an implacable and permanent force in my home state, was reduced to a slim majority in the Texas Senate and very little else. The transformation was even more far-reaching than the one that put the GOP, and George W. Bush, into power in 1994: it seemed more on par with the elections that ended reconstruction in Texas. After signing the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Johnson told his aide, fellow Texan Bill Moyers, that his party had “lost the South for your lifetime—and mine.” Moyers died last year.

The central stories of the Texas liberal tradition are the fall of man and the tower of Babel. There was an idyll once, or we tried to make one, and it fell apart because of—pick your poison—flaws in ourselves, flaws in others, flawed perception. The need for these narratives must reflect, on some level, self-awareness about the absurdity of trying to bring progress to a well-armed and bloody-minded garrison state called into being first to serve as a frontier between a long succession of empires and then to keep various arteries of global commerce flowing.

When the settlers arrive in the Texas Hill Country in the first pages of Robert Caro’s The Years of Lyndon Johnson, they find a garden, with ample water and fields of wildflowers. When they work the land, the soil slides off into the creeks. Something about their very presence has corroded the order of things and they’ll never get it back. Today these fields are covered in subdivisions. This is history as parable: we know these books are about a man who will eat the apple and acquire godlike powers—create his own idyll, the Great Society—and that it will break, just like all the others. This is on some level the story of, among others, the Fourierist socialists who helped settle Dallas, the German forty-eighter liberals who were cut down by Confederate militias for draft-dodging, the National Grange populists, midcentury union organizers, the glorious doomed one-term reign of Governor Ann Richards, and various failed Democratic campaigns through the present day.

One of the central texts of this tradition is Billy Lee Brammer’s The Gay Place (1961), a novel about lost idylls. Brammer wrote about his social circle in the 1950s, when Texas liberals had some real influence. The characters are all fallen in their own ways, except for Lyndon’s stand-in, who has his own eerie way of moving in the world. Putting him on paper lost Brammer access to the real thing. Cut off from a man who had become a kind of father figure and struggling to replicate the genius of his first book, Brammer spiraled, dying of an overdose in 1978.

Much of the action in the book takes place in a version of Austin’s Scholz Garten, a bar and restaurant founded 1866 just east of the state capitol, which has seen many generations of Texas dreamers come and go. Brammer would have been there with his wife Nadine Cannon, another famed Texas liberal. When they divorced she married the future congressman Bob Eckhardt. On the night before the election I walked from Scholz’s to a nearby music venue to hear their daughter, Sarah, speak, along with Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, and had for the first time the strangely out-of-body, out-of-time feeling that many Texans have been having this month.

Nadine’s daughter beat her opponent by more than five points, and he had a little meltdown on stage in Dallas, where he blamed every other Republican on the ticket. As he was doing so, Texans were flooding Austin, honking horns, cheering, setting off fireworks. It was the day of the dead. We’re giving it another go.

Will the Blue Wave Crash Against the Border Wall?

Francisco Cantú

The border town of Lochiel, Arizona, was once the lone port of entry along an eighty-mile expanse of rugged mountains and grassland valleys between Nogales to the west and Douglas to the east. When its customs house was shuttered in 1983, the small community effectively became a ghost town. This past summer it was descended upon by crews of workers from Fisher Sand & Gravel—a construction firm that since 2019 has been awarded billions of dollars in border wall contracts from the Department of Homeland Security. They had come to replace the current fifteen-foot barrier with a steel bollard wall that would be twice as high and double-layered with a strip of no-mans-land in between, designed to further impede human crossings despite the fact that this is one of the least trafficked corridors in Arizona.

Spanning the border at Lochiel is a grove of cottonwoods that has served for centuries as a riparian oasis for wildlife and migratory birds. On July 27 three of its largest trees were torn down to make way for the wall’s planned expansion. Just as a fourth and final tree was about to be removed, a woman named Kate Scott, who had caught wind of the destruction, arrived to protect it. Soon an entire community of activists arrived at the border, temporarily halting the crews and bringing the town back to life. Working together, they erected a platform in the canopy and mobilized a rotating group of land protectors in a “tree sit” that held the US government and its contractors at bay for the next seventy-one days. Armed agents finally swept the camp in the early morning of October 5, using a cherry picker to extract the on-duty sitter. This cleared the way for contractors to topple the ancient cottonwood, which the activists had taken to calling “grandmother.”

It has been a devastating and dystopic year of immigration enforcement. Masked agents have been deployed far from the border, occupying American cities and murdering citizens and noncitizens alike. Even Trump himself has acknowledged that the unpopularity of his administration’s crackdown contributed to the blue wave. The correlation is starkest in the Southwest, where for the first time since the 1970s all four border states have elected Democratic governors. Every House district that was up for grabs along the border swung blue. Seven of eight border state senators are now Democrats, too, with Ted Cruz the only Republican who remains. The shift is seismic—but will borderland Democrats deliver change?

The militarization of the border has long been a matter of bipartisan consensus. Even under Democratic majorities, there has never been serious discussion of shrinking the size or power of ICE and Border Patrol, the two largest federal law enforcement agencies in the nation. We would be wise to recall that Obama deported three times as many migrants as Bush, and that Biden tripled Trump’s expulsions, overseeing a twelvefold increase in detention at the border. Immigration enforcement has grown more lucrative and profitable than ever before, with vast amounts of personnel and huge sums of money dedicated to the proliferation of surveillance, incarceration, and deterrence. Under Democrats, rhetoric may be tempered and enforcement may become less visible, but profit motives and institutional inertia will remain.

In an analysis for the Tucson-based Border Chronicle, the journalist Todd Miller found that many borderland Democrats campaigned for Congress on a status-quo approach to immigration control—even high-profile candidates like the Tejano singer Bobby Pulido, who managed to flip a Republican seat in his Rio Grande Valley district, said that he supports “tougher border enforcement.” Others, like New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, have touted a tech-centric approach, advocating for autonomous surveillance towers and “smart” detection infrastructure. This, too, is nothing new—Democrats shouldn’t forget the enormous expense and spectacular failure of Boeing’s Secure Border Initiative Network (SBInet), the “virtual fence” project launched in 2006 and subsequently canceled by DHS after five years of glitches, delays, and ballooning costs.

A smaller handful of borderland Democrats—like Arizona’s Adelita Grijalva, who was pepper-sprayed by ICE earlier this year when she showed up to protest an immigration raid on a Tucson restaurant—have been more vocal in their repudiation of border militarization. Others, like San Diego’s Sara Jacobs and El Paso’s Veronica Escobar, have even voiced support for curbing the powers of DHS by increasing accountability and shrinking its size and funding. If these borderland Dems can influence their party’s traditionally hawkish centrists, they could help foment the most significant restructuring of immigration enforcement since September 11.

A few days after the final tree was torn down in Lochiel, I drove to the border to attend a vigil mourning its loss. Wall construction was in full swing, with contractors lowering giant steel panels into a moat of wet concrete, watched over by heavily armed and masked border guards. When I stood at the site where the last cottonwood had fallen, I realized that for many people it may be easier to imagine the steel and concrete of a wall than it is to picture this vibrant place, where trees teemed and diverse constellations of borderland residents came from afar to defend them. New construction often obliterates the memory of what was there before. But those gathered here were determined to look beyond the wall, convinced that the real harbinger of change wasn’t the monolithic structure itself but the fact that, for seventy-one days, its inevitability had been called into question by people audacious enough to fight against it.

The Foreign Is Domestic

Aslı Ü. Bâli and Aziz Rana

Within hours of the polls closing, Vice President JD Vance blamed the Republican rout on the Iran war. Most analysts understood Vance to be distancing himself from Trump and putting forward his own vision for the GOP. It was striking, then, that he explicitly tied foreign policy to pocketbook issues at home, framing every dollar spent on other countries’ problems as something taken from Americans. To win back Trump voters, he wrote in a statement on X, Republicans need to do four things: “1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel.”

Vance, who spent much of this year publicly boosting the war while allowing leaks to suggest he was an internal skeptic, may be a compromised antiwar messenger. Still, his post serves as a reminder that for over a decade “America First” politicians have been connecting foreign and domestic policy in a distinctive way. This has largely taken the form of pro-business protectionism and extreme anti-immigrant crackdowns. They have even advanced a vision of multipolarity, spelled out in the Trump administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy, which advocates a world organized around competing authoritarian hegemons, each extracting resources and immiserating enemies in its own sphere, as Trumpists have done in Venezuela and Cuba. Here and elsewhere, the “America First” crowd treats the international community with suspicion, scapegoats immigrant workers for the failures of the larger economic system, and advocates withdrawal from the Middle East in order to redirect the savings toward a fortress America, walled off from immigrants and foreign competition.

As Tuesday showed, voters across the political spectrum do indeed want lower costs and a different relationship between America and the world, and many see the two as connected. The midterms were the latest electoral rejection of American primacy—the belief that the United States should remain the world’s dominant power, sustained by force, sanctions, and military alliances—and its litany of costly wars. In Iran, these policies have destabilized the Gulf and damaged the global economy without producing submission, legitimacy, or a durable settlement; instead, this latest war of choice has driven up the price Americans pay for everything from gas to groceries.

But it is not enough for the Democrats to say that the war was reckless or promise better economic management. Unless they offer their own story of how the foreign and the domestic are joined, Vance’s account of why the Iran war was wrong will be the primary one on the table.

During the midterms, the closest thing to a rejoinder came from Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan. His broad platform was made in Bernie Sanders’s mold, with a focus on getting money out of politics, making life more affordable, and passing Medicare for All. He also openly denounced the Iran war and challenged the bipartisan consensus on Israel. And he linked these positions, arguing explicitly that the money being expended on war would be better spent on America’s children, schools, and health care system amid an affordability crisis. But his call to decrease military spending was paired with one to restore funding for international assistance programs, global health, and foreign aid. Contra America First’s case for walling off the country from global commitments while seeking to dominate a sphere of influence, El-Sayed argued for military restraint and rethinking the values our foreign policy advances. The two halves of his platform fit together: on both fronts he asked what ends America’s wealth ought to serve and answered with a politics of care at home and abroad. Tellingly, he faced nearly as much opposition from centrists in his own party as from Republicans.

El-Sayed’s establishment Democratic colleagues may be tempted to seek restoration abroad and revert to incrementalism at home. As the midterm results came in, Hakeem Jeffries declared, “America is back.” These Democratic leaders, holding firm to their belief in American primacy, may treat the Iran war as a uniquely Trumpist blunder, rather than what it was—a step on the disastrous path laid down by decades of American belligerence and regional hegemony in the Middle East. That would mean failing to offer the type of alternative that Americans are clearly calling for.

Democrats won this landslide because voters rejected Trump and the Republicans, helped by the same global anti-incumbent mood that aided Trump in 2024. But they cannot count on the specter of Trump to deliver future elections, especially past 2028. A Democrat elected president in two years may get no honeymoon before polarization and the Constitution’s many veto points close off the space for a reset. The window for a genuinely revised foreign policy and its necessary correlate, democratic reform and accountability, will be very small.

The urgency extends to the weeks before January. Americans and the world cannot wait two more months for the Iran war to end, especially as Trump routinely threatens to destroy Iranian civilian infrastructure—threats that all on their own are likely a war crime. Democrats should use the election result and Republican disarray to block any further illegal bombing and blockade, including by refusing to fund the government in the next continuing resolution as long as the war persists. Many changes will require a new president, but the window for demonstrating the seriousness of Democratic commitment opens now.

Over the next two years Democrats must connect affordability issues at home to the persistent ethical and legal failures of the national security state. The first way to do this is by insisting on accountability. Officials from both parties have long enjoyed effective impunity for state violence, treating war and immigration as sites for executive say-so and plenary power; Trump simply pushed the imperial presidency to its logical conclusion. In the process he made evident that violence carried out by the US government, both overseas and at the border, belongs to a system of defense contracts and capital flows that grossly enriches an empowered few, while most Americans—and, of course, the targeted populations themselves—bear the cost.

Congressional Democrats now have the leverage to reclaim what their institution has largely forfeited: its constitutional role as an independent check. Beyond this week’s Hegseth impeachment vote, they can demand hearings, subpoenas, war powers votes, and a full public accounting of the Iran war and its human costs. The same goes for the lethal strikes and military buildup in the Caribbean and Venezuela and the blockade of Cuba, and for the terror induced by ICE’s brutal rampage across the country. In this way foreign policy and democratic reconstruction can go hand in hand.

The second task for Democrats is to offer an alternative vision of America’s place in the world—one that answers the demands of their base and, increasingly, most Americans, and also competes with the America First version of multipolarity, which will otherwise fill the void. This would require an explicit rejection of American primacy in favor of a world order grounded in collective decision-making, a shared commons, and mutual self-restraint.

At a minimum, this new posture would involve rejecting elective and preventive wars, refusing to conduct policy by sanction and blockade, and investing in what actually produces security: climate, health, and constraints on oligarchic power, alongside multilateral engagement and legal compliance. Getting there will require, among other things, identifying and empowering a new generation of foreign policy thinkers to staff the next administration. The current bench in both parties is deeply implicated in the policies that have brought us to this moment. Breaking with longstanding bipartisan consensus will mean drawing on diplomats, arms control specialists, climate experts, and international lawyers whose expertise has been sidelined, rather than recycling yet again the same circle of think tank and defense-industry advisers.

This will be difficult, especially in a divided Democratic caucus whose leaders have little interest in asking where unconstrained US power has led the country and the globe. But Americans have voiced their discontent in terms unparalleled since Watergate. Democrats can spend the next two years in a protracted fight between moderates and progressives, waiting for the pendulum to swing back. Or they can use this fleeting moment to build a governing coalition that gives ethical meaning and political substance to their mandate.

These are the fifth through eighth entries in a symposium of responses to the 2026 midterm elections.

Rozina Ali • Olivia Paschal • Lily Geismer • David Treuer

‘Are You for America?’

Rozina Ali

In the fiery lead-up to the midterm election in Michigan, mailers arrived at voters’ homes bearing the gray-toned images of a woman in a burqa and Abdul El-Sayed’s face. The leaflet, sent by a Republican-aligned super PAC, warned that the Democratic candidate’s “Sharia-compliant way” would restrict women’s rights and freedoms. Grotesque as it was, it was a small drop in the deluge of tirades about El-Sayed’s ethnicity and faith, from right-wing commentators and sitting politicians alike.

His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, excoriated him for connections to the Muslim Brotherhood—an Islamist political group in Egypt that his mother once allegedly supported in the 1970s. Vice President JD Vance claimed that El-Sayed had “zero attachment” to the United States, though he was born and raised in Michigan. At a campaign event outside Detroit, Texas Senator Ted Cruz warned that if El-Sayed was elected and put on the Senate intelligence committee “there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result.” The dog whistles about how the first Muslim senator would threaten the Western way of life were so incessant and absurd as to become boring. Then there were the playground taunts: President Trump poking fun at his name, Cruz calling him a “jihadist leprechaun,” Louisiana Senator John Kennedy claiming he slept in a “bin Laden jersey.”

In some ways, this anti-Muslim bigotry was perfectly in keeping with the past two decades, when Islamophobia gradually became a feature of American election cycles. As more people were arrested inside the country on terrorism-related charges, the public’s fears became fodder for a new kind of politics. In 2008 a right-wing advocacy group called the Clarion Fund sent out DVDs to millions of voters in swing states warning about the dangers of radical Islam in the United States. Two years later local governments debated adopting anti-Sharia legislation, while a manufactured national controversy about plans to open an Islamic community center in lower Manhattan—which conservative opponents dubbed the “Ground Zero mosque”—seeped into the midterm elections. In 2016 Republican candidates competed to prove their anti-Muslim bona fides, calling for a ban on immigration from Muslim countries and extra monitoring of mosques. The Democrats, too, accepted Muslims only on certain conditions. “If you’re a Muslim and you love America and freedom and you hate terror,” Bill Clinton said on the DNC stage that year, “stay here and help us win and make a future together.”

Still, this year’s Michigan Senate race was arguably the most Islamophobic in US history. In the past, politicians have seemed to preserve a dichotomy between “good Muslims”—the assimilated, patriotic ones—and “bad Muslims”: the dangerous, radical members of the faith. This time, the distinction collapsed. El-Sayed’s opponents from both parties attacked him by questioning his loyalty and arguing that he doesn’t love his country—all but saying that a Muslim should not and cannot hold an influential office in the United States. “Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked during their second debate in October. El-Sayed’s rival in the Democratic primary, Haley Stevens, explaining her decision to switch sides and endorse Rogers at the eleventh hour, repeatedly accused El-Sayed of being “hateful.” “I’m choosing country over hate,” she announced at a press conference two days before the election. Voters were unmoved by the attacks. Despite more than $400 million spent in the Michigan race, mostly in favor of Rogers—what one journalist remarked was equivalent to a small nation’s GDP—El-Sayed beat his opponent by 7 points.

Gambling on Islamophobia as an electoral strategy was reckless: in the past, heightened anti-Muslim rhetoric correlated with an increase in anti-Muslim assaults nationwide. It was also astonishingly tone-deaf. In a moment when Americans’ medical debt has reached at least $220 billion and credit card debt is at an astounding $1.26 trillion, compounded by worsening inflation and rising gas prices, it’s not Islamic terrorism but affordability that Americans worry about.

El-Sayed was not just a Muslim candidate but a candidate who exhibited remarkable message discipline about these very points. A doctor who chose a career in public health and wrote two books about the possibility of national health care policy, he spoke exhaustively about Medicare for All. He also persistently tied the affordability crisis to the stupidity of Trump’s war with Iran and the billions going to fund Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

In this, he reflected a shifting tide: most of the country wants restrictions on aid to Israel, and a majority now favors a national health care plan. That El-Sayed’s opponents fell back on such old tropes—AIPAC spent more than $31 million attempting to cast him as an antisemite and a misogynist—was in itself a sign that they lacked substantive policy proposals of their own. In Equator, Nikhil Pal Singh convincingly argued that the midterm season’s “blue tsunami” spells the end of “9/11 as a font of reactionary politics.” After nearly two decades in which both Barack Obama and Donald Trump “rose to the top of their respective parties” by rejecting George W. Bush’s wars on the campaign trail, only to start new conflicts once in office, voters are less likely than ever to support the never-ending “war on terror.” 

Advertisement

This is not to say that Islamophobia is dead. Attacks against El-Sayed continue. His critics charge him with being “radical”—not just in reference to his supposed “ties” to an Islamist group in the Middle East but also because he wants to upend a status quo grounded in a longtime bipartisan consensus. Like a growing number of his colleagues on Capitol Hill, El-Sayed has been unequivocal in his critique of Israel as an apartheid state and his desire to stop funding for the country. As Senator-elect he has already voiced his support for a challenger to Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader—which inspired a joke about antisemitism from Saturday Night Live.

“I’m not running to be a Muslim senator, I’m running for the US Senate and happen to be Muslim,” El-Sayed said on the campaign trail. The line, of course, evoked John F. Kennedy, the first Catholic to be US president, who was questioned during his own election season about his loyalty to the pope versus the Constitution. It was a nimble and effective rhetorical move. But I also think of another moment from Kennedy’s political rise, when he famously urged the public in his inaugural speech to “ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.” The phrase inadvertently hemmed in our politics for decades, but this election cycle’s historic and remarkable swing leftward, among struggling Americans of every demographic, marked its repudiation. If the parameters of today’s politics are love and hate, then the underlying question isn’t so much which side loves their country more but whether the government loves its people.

The Changing of the Southern Guard

Olivia Paschal

The GOP’s twenty-first century Solid South was never quite so solid as it seemed. Florida, Tennessee, and Arkansas had some Democratic statewide representation until the 2010s. Georgia’s Senate seats flipped in 2021. North Carolina, Kentucky, and Virginia all currently have Democratic governors. Nonetheless, in the Trump era, offices that partisans had long hoped would turn entirely blue had remained stubbornly red through the campaigns of candidates like Stacey Abrams, Beto O’Rourke, and Jaime Harrison. On Tuesday night the dam finally broke, not only in Texas and the swingier North Carolina but also in the apparently deep-red states of South Carolina, almost certainly Mississippi, and, very nearly, Louisiana. The states of the former Confederacy no longer move as a bloc, but it is hard to look at Democratic victories throughout the Deep South and see anything other than a repudiation of the party that has held power, in some measure, for the last quarter century.

As the national Democratic party (and national progressive funders) backed away from many Southern states, local and regional organizers dug in. Their work has made the difference. In the second Trump term, grassroots organizing around the South has confronted issues like ICE arrests, data centers, and the right to the ballot. Black voters were mobilized by the Supreme Court’s Callais decision gutting the Voting Rights Act and by the heavy-handed racial gerrymandering Republicans had undertaken across the region; groups like Black Voters Matter and Stacey Abrams’s host of voting rights organizations have been building political infrastructure across the Deep South, including Mississippi, for years. Thousands of Black students marched to the polls from HBCUs like Jackson State and North Carolina A&T, where the Guilford County Board of Elections moved a polling location a forty-minute walk from campus despite student protests. Latino voters across the region swung left again, a response to the violent detentions ICE carried out in workplaces, on the side of highways, and even, as in Western North Carolina, at a swimming hole in a national forest, often at the invitation of Republican leadership.

Record turnout in the region shows just how much ground Republicans have lost. In North Carolina, where the well-liked former governor Roy Cooper beat a lackluster Trump candidate for the state’s Senate seat, 54 percent of voters went to the polls—the most since 1990. That high turnout also helped flip the state’s House delegation. In South Carolina, the Democrat Annie Andrews beat Lindsey Graham’s sister Darline by five points in an election that also set turnout records. Texas’s turnout was 5 percentage points higher than in the last midterms.

Advertisement

In some places candidates who barely campaigned won their seats because of the D by their name. Democrats flipped at least one chamber in the state legislatures of North Carolina and Texas, may have flipped the Georgia House, and broke Republican supermajorities in Florida, the Arkansas House, and the South Carolina House. Public boards and commissions also swung Democratic—including the Georgia public utilities commission, long a rate-hiking monopoly—as did local elections in places like Lynchburg, Virginia, home of Liberty University. In Huntsville, Alabama, home to a vast military-industrial complex, voters sent the first trans legislator in Alabama history to the statehouse. She beat the incumbent Republican by seven points.

Assessor races, county boards, the Texas state board of education—the changing of the guard in these kinds of offices heralds shifts not just in national policy but in the state-level policy that, thanks to organizations like ALEC and the Federalist Society, the GOP has held and weaponized for nearly two decades. It is these down-ballot races that may ultimately have the most impact on policies like Medicaid expansion, local police partnerships with ICE, and data center construction.

A Democrat, of course, does not a progressive make. Many of those who won statewide in the South are centrists. Keisha Lance Bottoms is best known in many parts of the progressive left for her insistence on constructing Atlanta’s Cop City during her term as that city’s mayor. Scott Colom, who may well flip a Mississippi Senate seat, highlighted his relationship with the police in his launch video. In Texas, James Talarico softened on trans rights as the GOP attacked him and Gina Hinojosa on well-trod culture war lines. Their victories, however, should still lessen the firehose of catastrophes that on-the-ground organizers have been combatting on multiple fronts since 2024.

The statewide candidates who won had one thing in common with others around the country: the focus on affordability, economic populism, and the growing gap between rich and poor. Colom’s launch ad showed him grocery shopping with his family, and his campaign promised to raise wages and work to end tariffs. Andrews’s platform included plans to protect workers’ rights, raise taxes on the wealthy, and reopen rural hospitals. Justin Pearson also focused on inequality in his campaign for the House in a formerly majority-Black district in Tennessee that had been extraordinarily gerrymandered by Republicans. He lost by just 2,500 votes. Workers and farmers across the South have been hammered by Trumpian tariffs, decades of anti-labor economic policies, and the continuing loss of rural hospitals and health care. It’s incumbent on newly elected Democrats to show they can offer something different.

All the stars aligned this cycle—a motivated electorate, high turnout, lackluster Republican candidates. The down-ballot wins in the South have given Democrats a chance to build a bench in states where they haven’t been competitive in a long time, and opened up the space to try out a new politics. But the success of that politics depends on whether the party and its newly elected candidates show voters that they can actually offer something new. It also relies on national Democrats investing in Southern states that, Tuesday showed, could be competitive—like Louisiana, where the Democratic Senate candidate Jamie Davis lost by less than 2 percent. If the blue turn is to be sustained, national organizations and funders will need to focus resources on the South again—so that the voters and organizers who pulled Democrats across the finish line can begin to see their efforts pay off.

Revenge of the Watergate Babies

Lily Geismer

The scale of the Democratic victory last Tuesday has sent pundits in search of historical comparisons. It easily surpassed 2018 and 2006 and even 1994, when Newt Gingrich led the GOP to control the House of Representatives for the first time since the 1950s. The closest analogy seemed to be 1974, when seventy-six new Democratic representatives entered the House and the party made major gains in the Senate and governorships. The group earned the label “Watergate Babies” on the assumption that it was anti-Nixon sentiment that drove them. Anger at Nixon and Watergate certainly contributed to their electoral success, but the label was a misnomer: their main target was less Nixon than the Democratic establishment, which they considered too bureaucratic, inefficient, and beholden to the labor movement. 

The Watergate Babies were predominately Ivy League-educated, white, male, and under the age of forty. Many of them came from the Sunbelt South, where they represented largely white, middle-class suburban districts. Most had never before held political office, but all promised to make government more efficient and transparent. The cohort included many figures who would become leaders in the Democratic Party for years to come, such as Paul Tsongas, Gary Hart, Michael Dukakis, George Miller, Henry Waxman, John Glenn, and Dale Bumpers. In his stump speech Hart railed against the Democrats for “throwing money at problems” by creating more federal programs or agencies. “It is time to replace the New Deal, or at least the conventional thinking which is its grandchild,” he declared.

Historians, myself included, have had much to criticize about the Watergate Babies’ influence on the Democratic Party since the 1970s: they worked, I have argued, to tilt the party toward suburban moderates and codified a market-based, tech-oriented economic policy agenda that created new forms of inequality and alienated working-class voters.1 The Watergrate Babies do, however, deserve credit for the ways they sought to check executive power, reform the institutions of Congress, and upend the Democratic establishment. The class of 1974 helped, among other things, to end the seniority system that had long dictated committee placements and chairs and to redistribute power in the House toward the elected leadership and subcommittees, where new members could assert themselves.2 These efforts were by no means perfect, but the group at least recognized that they had to make politics and government function more effectively before they could achieve their policy goals. 

The class of 2026 is far more heterogenous than its historical antecedent. If these midterms are any indication, the Democrats seem to have finally taken seriously Howard Dean’s idea as chairman of the Democratic National Committee in 2005 to develop a “fifty-state strategy” focused on expanding party infrastructure and candidate recruitment in every state. The idea was quickly dismissed by party operatives like Rahm Emanuel and Paul Begala, who said it amounted to “hiring a bunch of staff people to wander around Utah and Mississippi and pick their nose.” It turns out they can do a lot more than pick their noses. Indeed, they can shift the party away from its obsessive quest, since the era of the Watergate Babies, to win suburban moderates in swing districts, focusing instead on making the party’s electoral coalition more economically and geographically diverse.

Still, the class of 2026 would do well to heed parts of the Watergate Babies’ example. Politicians and pundits alike have wrung their hands for decades over polarization and gridlock within Congress, but the most recent session reached unprecedented heights of paralysis and fecklessness. It is time, then, to use the momentum from this election to reform the legislative branch and reclaim the institution’s power and authority. The new class can, for instance, work with existing members of Congress to reassert control of the power of the purse afforded to them by the Constitution to curb the funding of ICE as well as rein in spending on the Iran War, support for Israel’s war on Gaza, and backing for other military action around the globe. Congress can also embrace its war powers, which is another authority granted by both the Constitution and 1970s-era legislation.  

Some of the most substantial changes the Watergate Babies made to the structure of Congress itself—such as providing more power to the elected leadership and reforming the committee system to give less power to the committee chair—have to some degree been a victim of their own success. In more recent decades they have had a part in calcifying the power of the Democratic leadership, allowing figures like Nancy Pelosi and Hakeem Jeffries way too much say in dictating the party’s legislative agenda. The committee structure hasn’t been reorganized since the 1970s, and a Democrat-led Congress could modernize it by eliminating committees that no longer serve a crucial function and adding those that do.3 For instance, no central committee on technology currently exists. Creating one would not only bring Congress into the twenty-first century but also serve as a means of developing and asserting tech regulation.

Reforms of this kind could help address the issues that today’s new lawmakers most urgently need to attend to, from Big Tech and AI policy to health care and immigration. An updated committee system could also redistribute some power within the party from the leadership and give more progressive members of Congress one way to shape the party’s agenda. These types of actions are not as dramatic or headline-grabbing as impeaching the president and other top officials. But they would help restore trust in our political institutions, and they would be at least a step toward showing the American people that the Democratic Party stands for a vision of government focused on addressing their needs.

The Shoreline

David Treuer

I—an Indian, a novelist, critic, historian, and Barthesian “scriptor”—am disinclined by disposition and profession to provide hot takes. I do language and I do it long-form. So it should come as no surprise that I have few thoughts about the momentous firsts—in Minnesota, Texas, Georgia, New Mexico, Michigan. There was a blue wave. A “blue tsunami,” in the words of the mealy-mouthed Ted Cruz.

But there was a Trumpian wave in 2024 (and what color was that, anyway?). A Bidenian bluish wavelet in 2020. A red wave with Trump foam in 2016. A blue tide (but no wave) with Obama. The problem with waves is that they crash and recede. I am less concerned with their pattern than what all of them, ultimately, do to the shoreline and the land beyond.

And what of the shoreline, which is nothing less than the unworthy, illegitimate, illegal republic that has imposed itself on my tribal homelands and those of my tribal relatives since its birth in 1776? The shoreline is a system that has not served me and mine since then and it does not serve us now. That violent system (made of declarations of independence and otherwise, institutions, military might, cultural hegemony, and believers in all of it—nothing less than the Republic itself) has infected and shaped and adulterated my homelands, my tribe, and has circled back to adulterate and affect even its most ardent supporters.

The outgoing lawbreakers will not be missed by me. Their current replacements—Peggy Flanagan, Abdul El-Sayed, Keisha Lance Bottoms, James Talarico, Deb Haaland, the most prominent among the new and more diverse class of clearly better leaders and better people—are wonderful and promising and promisingly wonderful. And it’s early yet (these victories are not even a week old) but my eyes are on the prize: the system remains the same and it needs to change. As I write this ICE is still on my street, Nolan Wells is still dead, Israel is still perpetrating a genocide with my money, Bears Ears National Monument is still eviscerated, and homelands are still being clawed open for nickel and oil and copper. And we still live in a nation that has been imposed on my tribal nation, and that imposer-nation is still a place where all such things are possible.

I have children. And I have students. And I have a big, wild, raucous family—some chosen and some inherited. I tell them all, every chance I get, that I was not put on this earth to console or flatter. As for my students, I tell them at the beginning of the term that we have sixteen weeks in which to read (hopefully!) ten books. And the point of those weeks and those books is not to master the information in those texts. Rather, we will work hard, we will read, we will talk, and we’ll use those books and that time to think and see differently. If literature has any power at all—and I think this is true of life as well—it is to help us to see and think differently about the world we share and the other humans in it. At the end of this short note I would like to implore our new leaders (and all of the old ones, too, for that matter) to act similarly.

Waves come and waves go. But use the years of service to which you have committed yourselves and the tools of your trade (nothing less than the nation to which you are pledged and the citizens that comprise it) to see and think differently. What, practically, could that mean? It could mean remaking the system (of laws, of thought, of practice, of culture) such that you not only vote to restore Bears Ears but change the way it is administered so that it can’t be re-smalled after you’re gone. It could mean teaching white boys to be more concerned about the killing of black boys than about supposed encroachments on their own freedom. It could mean remaking the government itself into a place where the ledger of profits from arms sales doesn’t rhyme with that of children’s deaths in Gaza, and indeed where that ledger doesn’t exist at all. Only then will the shoreline itself change, and with it the dreamy land beyond those dunes.

entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

Since 2019 Joseph O’Neill has been writing essays for the Review exhorting the Democratic Party to play offense in the face of what was beginning to seem like an aversion to winning. So in November 2024, in the bewildering days after Donald Trump’s reelection, I wrote to O’Neill in search of a diagnosis of the Democrats’ ills and a prognosis for the country’s recovery. His assessment—“it’s our job to make Trump fail, fail again, fail worse”—inspired what has become a series of conversations in the two years since, aimed at figuring out how Democratic leadership might be pressured into mounting effective resistance to the president’s alarming authoritarianism.

Now that the Democrats have finally scored an unambiguous victory in the midterm elections, the question is no longer how they might regain power, but what they should do with it. With two more years to go in Trump’s second term, I wrote to O’Neill this week to take the measure of the “blue wave.”

Daniel Drake: For the first time since we started doing these interviews, there is good news to discuss. The Democrats’ midterm victory outpaced even the more optimistic polls, and made clear that there is enthusiasm for progressive causes in states like Texas that were long written off by the party. (And it is looking more and more likely that they will flip Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska, too.) How do you interpret this shift in political fortunes? What do American voters want?

Joseph O’Neill: It’s all quite extraordinary, in a wonderful way. The Republican Party brand has collapsed, and it’s hard to see it improving while Trump is in office. But it would be wrong, I think, to interpret what happened merely as a symptom of dissatisfaction with diesel prices, grocery prices, and so on. The magnitude of the results signals that something bigger is afoot. Americans are sick of the ruling class—its corruption, its incompetence, its unresponsiveness. They are angry and worried, not only about the cost of living, but about a national trajectory that’s leading us into a dystopia dominated by artificial intelligence, environmental destruction, and a kind of neo-feudalism. Their vote was not as much a materialist spasm as an act of the imagination. This is the nature of the mandate that Democrats have received. A mandate is a command, we sometimes forget. It is mandatory for Democrats to respond to the voters’ concerns. If they don’t, their party could soon suffer its own collapse.

Drake: I’d like to take a second to ask, for once, what do you think the Democrats did right this time? What can​ the national party take credit for?

O’Neill: So much depends on understanding as accurately as possible the forces that produced this historic electoral victory. It’s important, in our magnanimous euphoria, to not allow the national party leadership to misappropriate political credit.

The biggest, most popular Democratic themes of the election—cost of living, corruption, data centers, ICE, Big Tech, billionaires, the Iran war (and the US-Israel military partnership)—were popularized by the likes of Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani, then successfully taken up by gifted communicators such as Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Adam Hamilton in Kansas. “Affordability” aside, the party leadership has assented to this agenda with great reluctance, if at all.

I’ve read that Chuck Schumer should get credit for “recruiting” strong Senate candidates. But on inspection, his contribution is hard to discern. It hardly took unique skills to persuade established politicians such as Mary Peltola (Alaska), Roy Cooper (North Carolina), and Sherrod Brown (Ohio) to run in the most propitious cycle of their careers. Adam Hamilton, James Talarico (Texas), Josh Turek (Iowa), Peggy Flanagan (Minnesota), and Annie Andrews (South Carolina) self-recruited. El-Sayed and Troy Jackson (Maine) were not favored by Schumer, whose preferred candidates, disastrously, were the scandalously sore losers Haley Stevens and Janet Mills. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, led by Schumer appointee Kirsten Gillibrand, declined to support the left-wing Angie Nixon, possibly depriving her of a win in Florida. And Scott Colom, who seems poised to flip the Mississippi senate seat, names Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Raphael Warnock, not Schumer, as his earliest and strongest supporters.

To whom, then, does the credit belong? When the Republican Party finally blew itself up, it was devoured by a gigantic blue electoral creature—what one might term the ActBlue coalition. Made up of countless ordinary citizens, this grassroots coalition has for more than a decade sustained a listless Democratic Party by donating, organizing, protesting, fretting, and voting. Renée Good and Alex Pretti were two such citizens. The credit belongs to them.

Drake: Already, Hakeem Jeffries has indicated that, when he is majority leader, he may not pursue impeachment proceedings against Trump. Do you think it would be worth expending political capital on an effort to hold the administration accountable for its vast apparatus of corruption? Or ought the Democrats prioritize policy victories first?

Advertisement

O’Neill: We have huge Democratic majorities and a bunch of new political stars who are champing at the bit. There will be no shortage of political capital and no shortage of people ready and able to take action. It will be feasible and necessary to pursue legislative maneuvering (on the economy, health care, ICE, etc.) simultaneously with oversight investigations into government wrongdoing and corporate overreach. A two-year long drama of interrogation featuring Pete Hegseth, Jared Kushner, Elon Musk, Todd Blanche, Alex Karp, Sam Altman, the many Epstein protagonists, et al., would establish where the Democrats stand: the elites are not above the law, corruption and cruelty are unacceptable, democracy can work. Impeachment of the president doesn’t seem called for at this moment, but that could change if Trump’s misconduct worsens.

Drake: It seems clear that the “blue tsunami” was in large part due to voters’ rejection of Trump and not their affinity with the Democratic Party. What can Democrats do to prolong and strengthen their own electoral appeal?

O’Neill: That is a question of brand strength, which is a question of earning the public’s trust relative to the Republican Party, a big question that never goes away. For now, I’ll simply say this: the younger new senators—Talarico, El-Sayed, Hamilton, Andrews, Turek, and hopefully Colom—have terrific brand potential. Why? Because they are perceived to be authentic and incorruptible public servants who have the well-being of ordinary people on their consciences. If that perception is substantiated, Democrats will become more electorally resilient. The legislative substance—Medicare For All, higher minimum wage, billionaire taxes, anticorruption, and so on—will, almost by definition, require the party to turn strongly leftward. That probably won’t be possible without a new president in the White House. The big political drawback with focusing on “affordability” for the next two years is that Democrats won’t yet have the power to make life much more affordable for anyone.

The structural problem, on this question of electoral resilience, is that the political playing field remains tilted in favor of the Republican Party. Democrats can use their new power to significantly fix this, right now, in several crucial areas.

The presidency—The Electoral College system is antidemocratic and favors Republican presidential candidates. There are now enough state legislatures under full Democratic control for the passage of the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. First proposed in 2006, it is an interstate agreement that would compel state legislatures to award their electoral votes to the presidential candidate who won the popular vote. Make it happen.

The judiciary—Trump has appointed three Supreme Court justices. That’s more than enough. Any SCOTUS vacancy in these next two years should remain unfilled, pursuant to the McConnell precedent. No federal judge should be appointed who does not pass basic fitness-for-office tests: affirming the legitimacy of Joe Biden’s 2020 victory, affirming the correctness of Roe v. Wade, affirming the wrongness of Citizens United. Americans gave the Democrats a huge Senate majority precisely so that they could check the Republican agenda.

The House—The extraordinary margin of this midterm victory has obscured the fact that Republican gerrymanders will make it very difficult for Democrats to win the House again. It is exceedingly important that Democratic state legislatures reciprocate, and ideally surpass, the Republican gerrymanders. Perhaps that will incentivize the GOP to pass federal legislation banning partisan redistricting.

The Oligarchy—A handful of media billionaires (the Ellisons, the Murdochs, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, et al.) control much of our ideological environment. Pumping out right-wing disinformation and hatred, spending hundreds of millions of dollars on political campaigns, they are corrupting our elections and undermining democratic norms (the rule of law, fair elections, access to reliable information and good education, the culture and practice of science, basic equality, and so on). Meanwhile, deranged billionaires in the field of AI are imperiling our civilization, our humanity, and nothing less than the continued existence of homo sapiens. Americans of every political disposition are sick of it: on Tuesday, a large majority of Montanans voted to ban “artificial persons” like corporations and nonprofit organizations from contributing to political campaigns and funding PACs. This is the path that Democrats must follow, at every level of government. Despite the defeat of Proposition 40 in California, wealth taxes on billionaires must be pursued in multiple states, with interstate coordination and support from the national party. The oligarchs must be taken down. It’s no exaggeration, at this point, to say that it’s them or us.

Drake: A writer I follow observed:

Advertisement

Elections are just another moment, just another beginning. It’s only an end for the people who lose; the people who win then have to govern. The current reality is that while progressive orgs and organizers in the US have figured out several winning formulas for getting candidates on the ballot and then in office, they have yet to figure out a consistent mechanism for keeping their electeds in line once they’re elected.

Could you speculate on what a consistent mechanism for holding elected Democrats accountable to their campaign promises might look like? That is, how can the voters now ensure that a notoriously timorous party actually pursues the policies—universal health care, ending the war in Iran, cutting off funding to the Israeli war machine—it was elected on?

O’Neill: It’s a good question. First off, Democrats need to figure out who the speaker and the senate majority leader will be. A congressional leadership consisting of Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer could not be more emblematic of the failed political order that voters have just rejected. The concern is substantive, too: it is hard to see how these two creatures of the donor class can be trusted to do what voters have called for, which is precisely to bring to heel a donor class whose interests (in foreign policy, health care, AI, and so on) are in conflict with the interests of ordinary Americans. The likelihood is that the status quo will be perpetuated, at least for another two years. It will be up to the aforementioned ordinary citizens, yet again, to apply pressure to force our incorrigibly subservient Democratic leaders to act like a party mandated by a historic electoral majority. Grassroots uproar works. It is unlikely, for example, that Jeffries will again meet privately with Jared Kushner, as he did in the summer, reportedly to discuss the “common ground” between the parties. We still don’t know what was actually discussed at that face-to-face, which remains inexplicable to anyone who believes that there’s a difference between good and bad government.

Drake: One of the most surprising developments of the midterms—and of the off-year elections since 2024—has been the success of democratic socialists. After Tuesday, the mayors of New York City, Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., Seattle, and Providence will all be democratic socialists, a development that was hard to imagine before Trump’s second term. A great many Americans still profess distrust of socialism, broadly construed. Do you think these mayors, alongside the more prominent DSA and DSA-adjacent politicians like Bernie and AOC, can reverse the more than century-long American antipathy to a social safety net and government services?

O’Neill: It’s still unclear if we’re seeing a fundamental ideological shift or something more fleeting. Either way, it feels very good to live in Mamdani’s New York. Most significantly, to my mind, he and other young politicians are inspiring young people of every background to take an interest in political action. Voters under thirty turned out in huge numbers these midterms, and they seem to have swung left, hard. It’s very encouraging.
